newsitem.title: FRANCE: Few traces of Deng's years as labourer in France.
newsitem.headline: Few traces of Deng's years as labourer in France.

text.p: France heaped praise on Deng Xiaoping on Thursday but drew a veil over his formative years spent labouring in grimy French factories, where the man who became China's leader learned to hate capitalist exploitation.
Deng left China in 1920 as part of a work-study programme, arriving in the southern port of Marseille at the age of 16.
He spent the next five years in France, working, while studying, in a series of factories where he saw the seamy underside of capitalism.
Disenchanted with the system, he joined the French branch of the fledgling Chinese Communist Party in 1924 and quickly worked his way up the ranks of Chinese revolutionaries in Paris.
He was soon well known to the police, who tried to arrest him in January 1926 at his home in the working class suburb of Boulogne-Boulancourt, only to find that he had fled for Moscow.

His lessons in capitalism came during a 21-day stint at a Groupe Schneider steel plant in the central town of Le Creusot, a month in a Hutchinson shoe factory in nearby Montargis and a stint at a Renault car plant in Boulogne-Billancourt, on the edge of Paris, which was a breeding ground for labour militancy.
Few documents concerning Deng's life in France have survived and his former employers said they were unaware of any surviving fellow workers who remembered him.
The Hutchinson plant in Montargis, where he also attended the local lycee (high school), still exists, but the Renault and Schneider factories are both closed.
Company records at Schneider show Deng began work at its steel plant at the age of 16 years and nine months. He worked as a "laminator" and his salary was listed as a paltry 6.60 francs.
He was one of some 300 Chinese workers to toil at the plant during the early 1920s under two-year contracts, but most left after a few weeks or months, the company said.
Renault keeps a yellowing document bearing a photograph of the youthful future Chinese leader, identified as worker "82409A". His name was recorded as Teng Hei Hien.
It was unclear when he began work at the car plant, but he left in 1926 "to return to China", the form erroneously states.
"For us, he was an employee like any other," a Renault spokeswoman said.

Deng returned to France on an official visit in 1975, before he became China's supreme leader, but there was little sign that he nursed either an affection for or a grudge against the country where he once worked.
In official reactions, President Jacques Chirac described Deng as "one of the great figures of Chinese history".

In a message to Deng's widow Zhuo Lin, Chirac recalled that France had "greeted Deng Xiaoping on its soil in the early 1920s", along with several other future Chinese Communist leaders, including the late Premier Chou En-Lai.
But he made no mention of Deng's fleeing France in 1926 a few steps ahead of the police.
